claim: CGEL treats gradability and compatibility with very and too as evidence that a noun has acquired adjectival status.
evidence_summary: Bylinina accepts very McDonalds as a predicative but rejects these very McDonalds french fries. Gonzálvez-García documents nominal grading with several intensifiers.
finding: Degree modification can diagnose a gradable use. Independent tests are needed to establish conversion of a lexical item. CGEL’s a very Oxbridge accent adds distributional evidence for Oxbridge.
proposed_wording: Compatibility with very or too is evidence for a gradable use. Use independent morphological or syntactic evidence to establish whether a lexical adjective has developed.
traditional_parallel: CGEL rejects inferring adjective category from prenominal modifier function. Similar care applies when inferring the category of a word from the gradability of the phrase that contains it.
inference: Does compatibility with very or too establish lexical conversion, or can a construction supply the gradable interpretation?

evidence.source: Elizaveta Bylinina (2011). This Is So NP! Baltic International Yearbook of Cognition, Logic and Communication 6, article 8.
evidence.passage: Ch. 19 §3.3(b), p. 1643. CGEL uses compatibility with very and too as evidence for conversion of nouns to adjectives, with fun and Oxbridge as examples.
evidence.example: Very McDonalds is accepted in the predicative example [12b]. These very McDonalds french fries is rejected in [21a].
evidence.establishes: The predicative pattern can supply a scale for the nominal. The same expression lacks the prenominal distribution expected for an ordinary gradable adjective.

evidence.source: Francisco Gonzálvez-García (2014). “That’s so a construction!” Theory and Practice in Functional-Cognitive Space, 271–294.
evidence.passage: Ch. 19 §3.3(b), p. 1643. CGEL uses compatibility with very and too as evidence for conversion of nouns to adjectives, with fun and Oxbridge as examples.
evidence.example: The X is so N(P) family also admits other intensifiers, including very and too, with varying degrees of conventionalization.
evidence.establishes: The distribution motivates testing a construction-level account alongside lexical conversion. The study treats the transition from noun to adjective as gradual.
evidence.locator: Chapter abstract and discussion of the intensifier paradigms.
